prompt.context: Tuck Air is a Central American airline with a hub in Guatemala City. It runs a hub and spoke system, meaning all flights connect through its Guatemala Airport location. The airline serves both regional routes and long distance routes. Historically, the airline has been one of the highest margin airlines in the world, but has seen significant profitability declines in the last year. The airline's management team would like to understand what is causing this profitability decline and how to address it.
prompt.question: What is causing Tuck Air's profitability decline, and how should management address it?

clarifying_info.a: No, there have been no changes to cost structure.
No, Tuck Air is one of the most operationally efficient airlines in the world and will be unable to significantly cut costs further.

clarifying_info.q: Has the airline made any operational changes such as new destinations or aircraft?
clarifying_info.a: No, the airline has made no operational changes.

clarifying_info.q: Has the airline changed its pricing?
clarifying_info.a: No, the airline has made no pricing changes.
Yes. Attracted by Tuck Air's historically high margins, two competitors have recently entered the Central American airline market.

exhibits.title: Load factor
exhibits.shows: A chart displaying business class and economy class load factors for Tuck Air over time. The industry average load factor is 80%.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: load factor percentage (50–100%). Two lines: Business class and Economy class. Both lines start above 80% (industry average) and show a recent decline; the Economy class line has dropped more sharply than the Business class line.

exhibits.title: Economy customer feedback
exhibits.shows: Four quotes from economy class passengers describing their expectations and experiences with Tuck Air and competitor airlines.
exhibits.data: David (28): complained meal was poor, expected only peanuts and water. Paul (53): complained about screaming babies, no wifi, cheap wine; wishes company allowed business class but it is too expensive. Linda (48): would switch to Kellogg Air for 20% lower price; every dollar counts on family vacation. Sarah (37): willing to pay a little more for a comfortable seat and in-flight entertainment on longer flights; currently prefers Wharton Air.

exhibits.title: Cabin redesign
exhibits.shows: A table showing the proposed new cabin configuration for the Boeing 737-700 with three classes: Business, Premium Economy, and Economy. Columns show seats, average price, load factor, and revenue per flight.
exhibits.data: Business: 8 seats, $400, 80% load factor, $2,560 revenue. Premium Economy: 18 seats, $300, 80% load factor, $4,320 revenue. Economy: 126 seats, $175, 80% load factor, $17,640 revenue. Total flights per year: 215,000.

framework: Diagnose the revenue vs. cost driver of profitability decline
Identify the competitive dynamics causing the revenue shortfall (new low-cost entrants undercutting economy fares)
Quantify the revenue gap and set a target (80% economy load factor = industry average)
Identify levers to close the revenue gap (pricing strategy, ancillary fees, cabin segmentation)
Use customer research to prioritize levers and design a solution
Model the financial impact of the chosen plan and check against the revenue target
Assess risks and outline implementation steps

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1 shows business class and economy class load factors for Tuck Air over the last year. The industry average load factor is 80%. What do you discern from this data, and what type of competitors is Tuck Air facing?
questions.guidance: The exhibit shows load factors historically above the industry average, reflecting Tuck Air's strong competitive position. The recent drop is most pronounced in the economy cabin. This suggests Tuck Air is being undercut on price specifically in economy class by low-cost carriers (LCCs). The problem is a revenue generation issue. Any solution must focus on increasing economy cabin load factor and must involve a change in economy ticket pricing strategy.

questions.prompt: Tuck Air's leadership has decided it must increase economy class load factor to 80% (industry average) while maintaining 85% business class load factor. Given the aircraft and pricing data below, how much of a revenue increase would achieving 80% economy load factor represent? Tuck Air only flies 737-700 aircraft, 215,000 flights per year. Business class: 8 seats, $400 average ticket price. Economy class: 144 seats, $200 average ticket price.
questions.guidance: The candidate should be organized in recording the data and performing calculations. The revenue gap of approximately $1.2B is large and will require significant action. Candidates should then brainstorm levers: changing pricing, bag fees, food/beverage charges, wifi charges, etc.

math.setup: Calculate current revenue per flight vs. target revenue per flight, then multiply by 215,000 flights.
steps: Current business class revenue per flight: 8 seats x $400 x 85% = $2,720
Current economy class revenue per flight: 144 seats x $200 x 60% = $17,280
Target economy class revenue per flight (80% load factor): 144 x $200 x 80% = $23,040
Target business class revenue per flight (85% unchanged): $2,720
math.answer: Tuck Air needs approximately $1.24B in additional annual revenue to reach its 80% economy load factor target.

questions.prompt: Now that we have discussed options to regain lost revenue, how would you decide which levers will have the greatest impact?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify understanding customer preferences as the first step. Customer focus groups, questionnaires, and surveys will provide the necessary data. Provide the candidate with Exhibit 2. After reviewing customer feedback, the candidate should identify distinct customer segments: price-sensitive travelers (David, Linda) who want bare-bones service; value-conscious travelers (Paul) who want more comfort but are unwilling to pay a large premium; and premium economy travelers (Sarah) who will pay more for comfort and entertainment. The best course of action is to segment customers within the cabin into Business, Premium Economy, and Economy. Ticket prices and service levels should vary by cabin. The candidate should address whether Tuck Air can be all things to all people and what cabin segmentation options exist.

questions.prompt: Acting on the customer segmentation recommendation, Tuck Air has decided to redesign its cabin as shown in Exhibit 3. Additionally: a $25 bag fee for traditional economy fliers (70% will check 1 bag per flight); traditional economy fliers will be charged for food/drinks, generating a net revenue gain of $200 per flight; free wifi added for the entire plane at a cost of $100 per flight (not charged to customers). What is Tuck Air's expected annual revenue under this plan? Does it meet the ~$5.5B target?
questions.guidance: The candidate should be organized with data and calculations. Total revenue per flight should be built up from three components: cabin revenue, ancillary bag fees, and net food/wifi impact. The result exceeds the ~$5.5B target, validating the plan.

math.setup: Calculate revenue per flight from cabin redesign (Exhibit 3), add bag fee revenue, add net food/wifi revenue, then multiply by 215,000 flights.
steps: Cabin revenue per flight (from Exhibit 3): $2,560 (Business) + $4,320 (Premium Economy) + $17,640 (Economy) = $24,520
Bag fee revenue per flight: $25 x 126 economy seats x 70% checking bags x 80% load factor = $25 x 126 x 0.70 x 0.80 = $1,764
Net food/wifi per flight: +$200 (food charges) - $100 (wifi cost) = +$100
Total revenue per flight: $24,520 + $1,764 + $100 = $26,384 (casebook rounds to $26,404 using $24,540 cabin revenue)
math.answer: Approximately $5.68B in annual revenue, exceeding the ~$5.5B target.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers are available to Tuck Air to regain the approximately $1.2B in lost annual revenue?

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Lower economy ticket prices to compete with LCCs and drive volume
Offer promotional fares to stimulate demand on low-load-factor routes

categories.name: Cabin segmentation
ideas: Create a premium economy cabin between business and economy
Offer tiered service levels within economy (e.g. extra legroom rows)

categories.name: Ancillary fees
ideas: Charge for food and beverages in economy
Offer priority boarding as a paid upgrade

categories.name: In-flight services
ideas: Add wifi (free or paid) to attract business travelers and premium economy
Offer in-flight entertainment as a differentiator
Provide complimentary snack/drink in premium economy to justify price premium

categories.name: Customer experience
ideas: Conduct customer surveys and focus groups to identify willingness to pay
Use feedback to tailor service offerings by segment
Partner with hotels or car rental companies for bundled offers

recommendation: Redesign the cabin into three classes — Business, Premium Economy, and Economy — with pricing and service levels matched to distinct customer segments identified through customer feedback

Implement ancillary revenue streams including bag fees ($25 for economy) and food/beverage charges for traditional economy, partially offset by a free wifi investment, to drive total annual revenue to approximately $5.68B and exceed the $5.5B target
risks: Competitors may redesign their own cabins to offset Tuck Air's advantages
Competitors may further cut prices, eroding the volume benefit of cabin segmentation
Customers may react negatively to new fees (bags, food) and switch to lower-cost competitors
Implementation complexity: reconfiguring aircraft cabins requires capital investment, maintenance downtime, and staff retraining
Brand risk if service quality in the new economy cabin falls short of expectations
next_steps: Trial the cabin redesign and ancillary fee changes on a subset of routes before network-wide rollout to test customer response
Conduct customer research (focus groups, surveys) to validate willingness to pay at the new price points
Develop a competitor monitoring process to track LCC pricing responses
Build a detailed implementation roadmap including aircraft reconfiguration schedule, staff training, and marketing communications
